title: Excuse Me, Can I Just Say…?

steps.html:
A councillor is explaining a plan and two people want in. Neither of them simply starts talking, and the way they get in is worth learning. Then a Norwegian town that spent half a million dollars on three mirrors.

  • Hear how English speakers get into a conversation
  • Interrupt without sounding rude, and hold your turn
  • Watch a documentary about a town without sunlight
  • Write a short, factual report

steps.title: When is it acceptable to interrupt?

options.label: When you have direct experience of what is being discussed
When the speaker has been going on too long
When you are the most senior person present

steps.title: Which interruption is most polite?
options: Sorry, that's wrong — you've misunderstood the proposal.
If I could just interrupt a second, I think that …
Wait a moment, would you listen to what I'm saying?
steps.answer: If I could just interrupt a second, I think that …
steps.why: It asks permission, names what it is doing, and takes only a second. All five phrases in this lesson do the same three things.

steps.title: Study the words.
steps.sub: Seven items — the smallest set in the level. The functional language after them is where the work is.

words.def: A group elected to run a town or area. Note the spelling: counsel is advice.
A district of a town with a particular character or trade.
To give the main points of something briefly.
To bring something to an end; also, to dress warmly.
At the beginning, before things changed.
A yearly book of calendars, tides, sunrise times and similar tables.
To stop. Formal, and common in writing.

steps.title: Before you listen: you are in a meeting and the speaker has a fact wrong.

options.label: Write it down and raise it later

steps.title: Listen. What is the meeting about?
options: A proposed new food quarter in Regent Court.
The closure of a local restaurant.
steps.answer: A proposed new food quarter in Regent Court.
steps.why: 'The proposed new food quarter will be in Regent Court.'

steps.title: Listen again. True or false?
steps.prompt: Several large restaurant chains have expressed interest.
steps.why: 'We have had quite a few expressions of interest from big restaurant chains.'

steps.title: Listen again. True or false?
steps.prompt: The first person to interrupt is entirely happy with the proposal.
steps.why: 'I have to say I'm not very happy about the proposal because of the noise.'

steps.title: Listen again. True or false?
steps.prompt: The second person to interrupt is a local restaurant owner.
steps.why: 'Can I just say that I'm a local restaurant owner…'

steps.title: Listen again. True or false?
steps.prompt: The councillor lets the discussion open up immediately.
steps.why: 'Just a second. Before we open the meeting up to everyone, I'd just like to explain my reasons.'

steps.title: Who says what?
steps.prompt: 'If I could just interrupt a second …' is said by …
steps.why: He goes on to ask whether local owners are wanted as well as chains.

steps.title: Who says what?
steps.prompt: 'Just a second.' is said by …
steps.why: She uses it to stop the interruptions and finish her explanation.

steps.title: Who says what?
steps.prompt: Why does the councillor mention the empty shop units?
options: To explain her reasons for proposing the food quarter.
To answer the restaurant owner's question.
steps.answer: To explain her reasons for proposing the food quarter.
steps.why: 'I'd just like to explain my reasons… quite a few of the shop units are currently empty.'

steps.title: Coming in, or holding the floor?
steps.sub: Listen to the phrases first if you want. Tap a phrase, then tap a column.

items.text: If I could just finish what I was saying, …
I'd like to say something, if I may.
If I could just interrupt a second, …

steps.title: Listen to the second meeting and answer.
steps.prompt: What had been agreed at the previous meeting?
options: To raise as much money as possible for charity.
To hold a vote on the food quarter.
steps.answer: To raise as much money as possible for charity.
steps.why: 'We agreed that we would try and raise as much money as possible for charity.'

steps.title: Listen to the second meeting and answer.
steps.prompt: What does the first interrupter ask?
steps.why: 'Excuse me for interrupting, but can I just ask when the last meeting was?'

steps.title: Listen to the second meeting and answer.
steps.prompt: How does the chair respond to the third interruption?
options: She agrees immediately and drops her own proposal.
She reclaims her turn: 'If I could just finish what I was saying …'
She ends the meeting and postpones the decision to next month.
steps.answer: She reclaims her turn: 'If I could just finish what I was saying …'
steps.why: That phrase is the counter-move to an interruption, and worth having.

steps.title: What do all the successful interruptions have in common?
steps.sub: Look at the pattern rather than the words.
options: They begin with an apology or a request, then say what they want to add.
They begin with the speaker's name.
steps.answer: They begin with an apology or a request, then say what they want to add.
steps.why: Permission first, content second. That order is what keeps an interruption from sounding rude.

steps.title: Habits, adjectives and adverbs in factual description
steps.html:
Recycled from Lessons 21 and 22, and now aimed at the report you will write.

A report describes a situation. That means the present simple for what is normally the case, the past simple for what happened, and used to for what has stopped: The town lies at the foot of a mountain. Work began in 1908. Residents used to leave the valley to see the sun.

Reports are dense in adverbs of degree, because a fact usually needs sizing: the temperature rarely exceeds −5°C, the light is considerably weaker, roughly six hours of daylight.

Keep the adjective/adverb rule from Lesson 21 in view. After be, become, remain, appear, use an adjective: The valley remains dark, not remains darkly.

A report also needs the passive, because who did something is often not the point: Three mirrors were installed in 2013. The scheme was funded by the company.

Finally, reports summarise rather than narrate. Prefer The council agreed to postpone the vote to a blow-by-blow account of who said what.

steps.title: Example bank.
steps.html:
Ten sentences in report register.

The town lies at the foot of Gaustatoppen.
Present simple for a permanent fact.

It was founded in 1908.
Passive past — the founder comes later, if at all.

Residents used to take a cable car out of the valley.
A habit that has stopped.

The winter temperature rarely exceeds −5°C.
Adverb of frequency sizing a fact.

There are fewer than six hours of daylight in mid-December.
Fewer than with a countable noun.

The reflected light is considerably weaker than direct sunlight.
Degree adverb + comparative.

The valley remains dark from October to March.
Adjective after remain.

Three mirrors were installed on the mountainside.
Passive; the installer is irrelevant.

The scheme cost roughly half a million dollars.
Roughly before a figure.

The council agreed to postpone the decision.
Summarised, not narrated.

steps.title: Turning three notes into one report sentence
steps.html:
1. The notes: mirrors — mountainside — 2013 — three of them — 17 square metres each — computer in Germany controls them.
  2. Decide what matters. The mirrors matter; who installed them does not. That means the passive.
  3. Put the facts in one clause each, and size them: Three mirrors, each of seventeen square metres, were installed on the mountainside in 2013.
  4. Add the control system as a separate sentence, again passive: They are controlled by a computer in Germany.
  5. Check the register. No you, no exclamation, no narrative. A report tells the reader what is the case, and stops.

steps.title: A Town in the Shadows
steps.sub: A Town in the Shadows. About seven minutes.

steps.title: Answer the questions about the film.
steps.prompt: Why does Rjukan lose the sun for six months?
options: Because of its latitude alone, like everywhere else that far north.
Because of the town's geography — it lies deep in a valley below a tall mountain.
Because of the cloud that sits over the valley all winter.
steps.answer: Because of the town's geography — it lies deep in a valley below a tall mountain.
steps.why: 'It is the result of the town's geography.' The mountain is Gaustatoppen.

steps.title: Answer the questions about the film.
steps.prompt: Why does the town exist at all?
options: It began as a farming settlement on the floor of the valley.
It was founded in 1908 around a hydroelectric plant built at a waterfall.
It grew up around a ski resort built for visitors from Oslo.
steps.answer: It was founded in 1908 around a hydroelectric plant built at a waterfall.
steps.why: Sam Eyde's company Norsk Hydro built what was then the world's largest hydroelectric plant.

steps.title: Answer the questions about the film.
steps.prompt: What was the solution before the mirrors?
options: A cable car, paid for in 1928, to take residents up out of the shadow.
Street lighting strong enough to work by through the winter.
Nothing at all — residents simply went without for six months.
steps.answer: A cable car, paid for in 1928, to take residents up out of the shadow.
steps.why: Eyde had the mirror idea as early as 1913 but had neither the resources nor the technology.

steps.title: Answer the questions about the film.
steps.prompt: How does the artificial sunlight compare with the real thing?
steps.why: Three 17-square-metre mirrors, controlled by a computer in Germany.

steps.title: Complete the notes from the film.

items.before: 3 — The mirrors were revisited as an idea by an artist in
4 — The mirrors cost about half a

steps.title: Read between the lines.
steps.prompt: Why does the film mention that not everyone thought the mirrors were worth the money?
options: To argue that the project was a mistake and should not have gone ahead.
To concede the objection before answering it with what the mirrors actually did for people.
To explain why the project took so many years to be approved.
steps.answer: To concede the objection before answering it with what the mirrors actually did for people.
steps.why: The next sentences describe faces brightening, teachers bringing students, older people meeting friends — the answer to the objection, not a retreat from it.

steps.title: Write a short report.
steps.sub: 160–190 words on Rjukan: the problem, the history, the solution, and how it has worked. Report register — no you, no exclamations, no narrative.
steps.html:
• Paragraph 1: the situation now, in the present simple.
  • Paragraph 2: the history, in the past simple and the passive.
  • Include one <i>used to</i> for something that has stopped.
  • Paragraph 3: the solution and the result, with at least two figures.
  • No second person, no exclamation marks, no dialogue.

Useful language

  • The town lies … and the sun does not reach it between … and …
  • It was founded in … , when …
  • Residents used to … , which meant that …
  • Three mirrors were installed in … , at a cost of …
  • The reflected light is considerably weaker than …
  • The scheme appears to have …
steps.modelHtml:
Rjukan: the mirror scheme

Rjukan lies at the foot of Gaustatoppen, in the Vestfjord valley, and receives no direct sunlight between October and March. The winter temperature rarely exceeds minus five degrees, and there are fewer than six hours of daylight a day in mid-December. The problem is geographical rather than climatic.

The town was founded in 1908 by the industrialist Sam Eyde, whose company built what was then the world's largest hydroelectric plant at the 104-metre Rjukan waterfall. Eyde proposed mountain-top mirrors as early as 1913, but neither the resources nor the technology existed. A cable car was funded instead, in 1928, and residents used to take it out of the valley in order to see the sun.

In 2013, three mirrors of seventeen square metres each were installed on the mountainside and are controlled by a computer in Germany. The reflected light is roughly twenty per cent weaker than direct sunlight. The scheme cost around half a million dollars and has been widely used since.
